## The Purpose of a Licence

Open-sourcing a project reverses the default "all rights reserved" model of copyright. A licence
formally communicates the rights that you, as a copyright holder, grant to others for the use of your
work. Without a licence, others have no legal right to use, copy, modify, or distribute your code —
even if it is publicly visible on a repository hosting platform.

Licence selection significantly influences a project's lifecycle and its external adoption.

## Software Licence Categories

Three primary software licence categories exist:

**Permissive Licences** (Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, MIT)
: Recipients may modify, combine, and distribute code freely, including in proprietary products,
  requiring only basic conditions such as copyright attribution. These licences maximise adoption and are
  the most common choice in academic and research software.

**Weakly-Reciprocal Licences** (LGPL-3.0, LGPL-2.1, MPL-2.0)
: Derivative distributions must disclose the original code under the same licence, but users of the
  derivative work are not required to open their own sources. Suitable for libraries intended to be used
  from proprietary software.

**Strongly-Reciprocal Licences** (GPL-3.0, GPL-2.0)
: Anyone who combines this licensed code with other code must release all sources — both the original
  and the derivative — under the same licence. Ensures that all improvements remain in the open-source
  commons.

## Choosing a Licence

The choice of licence should reflect:

- **Community norms** within your technology domain (e.g., most scientific Python tools use permissive
  licences; many Linux ecosystem tools use GPL)
- **Desired sharing regime** — whether you want to maximise adoption (permissive) or ensure that
  improvements are always shared back (reciprocal)
- **Institutional or project-level policies** set by CERTH or the funding body of your project (e.g.,
  Horizon Europe projects are encouraged to use open licences)
- **Consortium obligations** — multi-partner projects may have agreed-upon licence constraints in their
  grant agreement

When in doubt, consult the CERTH OSPO before publishing.

## Documentation Licences

For documentation and written outputs, the recommended licence family is **Creative Commons**.
[CC-BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) allows broad reuse with attribution and
aligns with European Open Science principles and most research funders' requirements, including the
European Research Council (ERC) and Horizon Europe.

For datasets, consider [CC0 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) (public domain
dedication) or CC-BY 4.0, depending on whether attribution is required by your institution or funder.

## European Context

The [EUPL-1.2](https://joinup.ec.europa.eu/collection/eupl/eupl-text-eupl-12) (European Union Public
Licence) is worth particular attention for CERTH projects. It was designed for European public bodies
and is explicitly compatible with several major copyleft licences including the GPL and AGPL, making it
a natural choice when interoperability with other European public-sector software is a priority.

See the [Licensing Recommendations](../recommendations/licensing.qmd) page for concrete guidance on
which licence to choose for your specific project type.
